children: An appointee of President Donald Trump will determine whether to end the American Bar Association's status as the federally recognized accreditor of US law schools after a US Education Department panel failed to deliver a recommendation on Thursday.

An 18-member agency advisory committee deadlocked on the question after a full day of debate on Wednesday that was marked by complaints of political interference and uneven rule enforcement. Education Department Under Secretary Nicholas Kent is expected to make the final call on the ABA legal education council’s accreditor recognition in the coming months.

“We take accreditation and our recognition as an accreditor very seriously,” Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA’s legal education council, said in a statement on Thursday. "We will continue to work cooperatively with the Department as the recognition process continues.”
The Education Department said it would not comment while a decision is pending.

The standoff over accreditation comes amid a wider political conflict surrounding both the ABA — the country's most-recognized attorney organization with about 150,000 dues-paying members — and its legal education council, which largely operates separately.

The Education Department in August recommended against renewing the ABA’s accreditor status, concluding that the ​legal education council is not "separate and independent" from the larger ABA as required. The staff report also faulted ​the ABA for being too slow to revise requirements related to law schools' diversity policies.

Trump signed an executive order in April 2025 directing Education Secretary Linda McMahon to assess whether to suspend or terminate the ABA as the government’s official law school accreditor, citing its “unlawful" DEI requirements. Under rules the ABA repealed earlier this month, its accredited schools were required to demonstrate their commitment to diversity in recruitment, admissions and student programming.

During debates on Wednesday before the Education Department's National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity, ABA critics on the committee argued that the real-world impact of ending its accreditor status would be modest because only five law schools rely on the ABA for access to federal student loans.

ABA supporters countered that it would upend US legal education by creating a patchwork of state lawyer licensing rules and argued that the government's accreditation standards were being unevenly applied to single out the ABA.
